title: Visual docs and self-updating roadmap
eyebrow: house-rules plugin · two new skills for any house-rules repo · revised for the review command · nothing built yet
approval: Design approved: visual docs and visual roadmap skills

short.lead: Proposal: two new house-rules skills for any repo with house rules docs. Visual-docs makes one illustrated overview page from the tier docs. Visual-roadmap redraws two roadmap views on your own machine when issues or merges change, with no GitHub Action of its own and GitHub Pages as an option. I need your approval and ten picks.
short.hint: Tap a step to see what it produces and what it needs from you.
items: Text docs and a hand-edited roadmap

Every house-rules repo has six tier folders (landing, roadmap, state, systems, today, decisions) and a hand-edited docs/2-roadmap/Roadmap.md. In this repo, the first one the skills will be tried on, there is also one plain-English copy so far (docs/plain/4-systems/hook-engine.md), and the roadmap is organised as eight phases worked in order (decided 2026-11-09). Nothing draws a picture, and nothing updates when an issue closes. The visual-loop skill already checks looks with a reviewer helper. The review command (planned, not yet merged) adds /house-rules:review with code, codebase, image and style modes.

items: Reading issues needs the gh command-line tool logged in; without it the script stops and says it cannot read issues (untested on your machine). In a cloud session the local files and the data file's history vanish when the session ends; only publishing to the roadmap-view branch keeps them. A change made in the browser appears only at the next refresh. GitHub Pages publishing is untested here, and I have not verified whether branch-based Pages draws on your Actions allowance, so it stays off by default. A repo whose labels or branch names differ from the defaults must set them in its settings file, and In dev stays empty until the dev branch named in the settings exists. Also: the review command is planned, not built (its parent issue 617 and steps 618 to 621), so both skills wait on it.
I run both, then you look

I run each on this repo and on a second house-rules repo you name, screenshot the output in light and dark at phone width, and add cases to verify.py. Done when three things hold. After gh issue create, gh issue close and gh pr merge into main, the session refresh shows each change on the local racetrack page within 60 seconds. /house-rules:visual-docs stale names a section after one of its docs is edited. /house-rules:review image mode returns the verdict clean on screenshots of each skill's output at 375px wide, in light and dark.
Name a second house-rules repo, ideally one with different labels, no dev branch or no Roadmap.md milestones, and give me access to it. Then look at the overview page and the two roadmap views.
A dated entry in docs/6-decisions/Decisions.md, one parent issue and one child issue per step.
Pick under Your choices and send the approval line.

changes: new
Skill 1: visual-docs
One illustrated page that reads like a game design document, built from the tier docs.

In any repo that has the six tier folders (a repo missing any is told which ones, and pointed to the project-docs skill), the skill reads docs/1-landing, 2-roadmap, 3-state and 4-systems, and the plain copies under docs/plain/ where one exists; for a doc with no plain copy it writes the plain wording itself. It writes one page to docs/generated/overview.html, the folder the tier rules keep for tool-made pages, and adds a link to it from docs/1-landing/README.md; tell me if you prefer another path. The page has six sections: the pitch in one line, the pillars (what the project promises), how it works as diagrams, each part and its state, the road ahead, and risks. Wording is for a person who has never opened the repo: no file paths in body text, jargon defined on first use. It reuses make_page.py's picture handling and colours (each repo's own docs/page-style.json; with none, the builder's default colours). Before finishing, it checks the page's wording and runs /house-rules:review image mode on screenshots of it, and the review command saves the report. Which page template it uses, and when the review runs, are your picks below.
plain-docs writes text copies only; make_page.py builds handover pages (proposal, build plan, QA, review, art); neither makes a project overview.
A new skill folder, one page layout, and a staleness check that mirrors plain-docs' stale mode.
You get a one-page, picture-led overview per project, regenerated only where the docs changed.

changes: new
Staleness check for the docs page
Flags sections whose source doc changed since the page was built.

Each section records a fingerprint (a short code that changes whenever the file changes) of the docs it was written from. Running /house-rules:visual-docs stale compares fingerprints and prints the sections to redo. A source doc that has gone missing is reported by name rather than skipped.
plain-docs already tracks staleness for text copies.
The same idea, applied to the visual page.
The page never silently drifts from the docs.

changes.alt: A source doc's saved fingerprint is compared on each run; a mismatch flags the page section as stale.
changes.caption: Mock-up of the staleness check.

changes: new
Skill 2: visual-roadmap
Two live views of the roadmap, redrawn by a local script; no GitHub Actions.

The script reads the repo's issues and pull requests through GitHub's REST API with gh api, because gh issue list is refused in Claude Code cloud sessions (tested 2026-11-24). It then rewrites one data file. It then redraws both views from that file. Each stage is matched by one or more labels set in the settings file. This repo's labels are the defaults, as an example: in progress is Doing, and needs review or in review is Review. An issue with none of the stage labels is Backlog, and one with two counts as the later stage. Install lists any label in the settings that the repo does not have, so a typo cannot quietly turn every issue into Backlog. A merge into the dev branch moves the issues its description closes (Closes #n) to In dev. A Part of link moves nothing. A merge into the release branch (a setting, default main) moves them to Shipped. An issue closed as not planned leaves the views. Where an issue closed as completed with no merge goes is your pick below. A lock file stops two quick refreshes from overwriting each other. Each trigger starts the refresh in the background and returns at once, so no hook waits on GitHub.
Four things start a refresh, and none of them is on GitHub. The plugin's session hook runs it after an issue is created, closed or relabelled, or a pull request is merged, in a session (gh issue create, close or edit, gh pr merge, or the GitHub tools' issue_write or merge_pull_request). A git post-merge hook runs it after a pull or merge. Starting a session runs it once, which catches changes made in the browser. /house-rules:visual-roadmap update runs it on demand.
Branch names are settings for each repo, because repos differ. This repo, for example, has no dev branch: no branch on GitHub was named dev when checked on 2026-11-24. There the In dev stage stays empty, and the view says why: no branch named dev was found. Run /house-rules:visual-roadmap install in any repo with house rules docs. A repo missing any of the six tier folders is told which ones and pointed to the project-docs skill. Install adds a settings file (dev and release branch names, the labels for each stage, a milestone mapping, publishing on or off) and a new git post-merge hook. The hook is added after any existing one, never in its place, and it respects core.hooksPath. Session start reinstalls it on a device that lacks it. Nothing in the skill is tied to this repo.
docs/2-roadmap/Roadmap.md is edited by hand; the issue labels already say whose move it is.
One script, one settings file, one data file, two generated picture files and a git post-merge hook. No GitHub Action.
The roadmap stays current on your own machine without drawing on your Actions allowance, and shows what is only in dev and what has shipped.

changes: new
View 1 (suggested): racetrack
Every issue is a dot on an oval track that ends at main.

Each issue is a dot. Its position on the track is its stage, so a crowded corner shows a bottleneck. The finish line is a merge to the release branch (default main). Each dot is labelled with its issue number, and titles appear beside it on a wide screen or as a list under the track on a phone. Dot colours are explained in a legend.
No visual view of issue flow exists.
A generated picture file (SVG).
You see where work is piling up.

changes: new
View 2 (suggested): burn-up chart
Three lines over time: opened, in dev and shipped.

The gap between the opened line and the in-dev line is work not yet merged; the gap between in-dev and shipped is work waiting for a release to main. It is the clearest picture of the dev-versus-main split. The opened and shipped lines are rebuilt from GitHub on the first run; the in-dev line starts the day the skill is first run.
No view shows how many issues were opened, merged and shipped over time; each repo's docs/2-roadmap/Roadmap.md gives each milestone a percentage and an acceptance test.
A generated line-chart picture file (SVG) built from the data file's history.
You see pace and the size of the unreleased pile.

changes.alt: A line chart over time with three rising lines: issues opened on top, issues in dev in the middle, issues shipped to main at the bottom.
changes.caption: Mock-up of the burn-up chart. Numbers are made up.

changes: new
Where the output is written
Local files by default; GitHub Pages is an optional extra.

By default the script writes to docs/generated/roadmap/ in the repo. That is one HTML page showing both views, where hover works, plus the two picture files. The install command adds a line to .gitignore so refreshes cause no commits.
With publishing switched on in the settings file, the script also pushes the same files to a roadmap-view branch, never to main, so the rule that main changes only by pull request holds. GitHub Pages then serves that branch as a public web page (unverified here). A private repo needs a paid plan for Pages. The script tries to switch Pages on with gh api and says so if it cannot. The data file is the only source of truth, and the views can always be rebuilt from it.
The repo rule: main only changes by pull request; docs/generated/ already holds generated files in this repo.
Local files by default; one extra branch only when publishing is on.
Main's history stays clean of auto-generated commits.

changes.alt: The script always writes local files. If publishing is switched on, it also pushes them to a roadmap-view branch that GitHub Pages serves. Publishing may start GitHub's own Pages deploy run (unverified).
changes.caption: Mock-up of where the output is written.

changes: new
What the review command gives these skills
Both skills reuse the reviewer; no new critic agent is made.

This revision assumes the branch AjsAgent/jolly-dirac-fvh4cg is merged and its parent issue 617 and steps 618 to 621 are built. That adds /house-rules:review and four reviewer modes: code, codebase, image and style, beside the existing page, plan, acceptance and diff. Reports are saved under docs/qa/review-<target>-<date>/. The design review loop decision of 2026-11-24, answer 4A (extend the reviewer, never duplicate it), still holds, so neither visual skill adds an agent.
Visual-docs checks its finished page's wording the way you pick below (the editor helper is suggested). It uses image mode on screenshots of that page at 375px in light and dark, because its pictures sit inside the page and have no file of their own. Visual-roadmap runs two reviews on each of its two pictures when it is built: image mode, and style mode with the stated style passed as criteria text (the legend's colours and the stage names). The review command's plan has not yet decided whether image mode accepts .svg files. The roadmap script runs without a Claude session, so that review happens at build time only, never on each update.
The reviewer has modes page, plan, acceptance and diff today; visual-loop uses it on screenshots; the review command is designed and planned, nothing built.
Nothing new here: this item only records what the two skills reuse once it lands.

Each review costs 75 seconds and 50,000 tokens (rounded averages of two measured page reviews). Visual-docs runs two or more per build (a wording check, then an image review of screenshots), and visual-roadmap runs four once, when it is built (two reviews on each of its two pictures). Only page reviews were measured, so the cost of these two kinds is unmeasured until the review command exists.

choices: c1
How fresh should the views be?
A
Also refresh on your next prompt, at most once every 5 minutes (suggested)
During a session the views are never more than 5 minutes behind. Between sessions they stay as old as the last session.
B
The four triggers only
A change made outside a session can stay unseen until the next session start, pull or update command, with no upper limit.
C
Add a local scheduled job (cron or Task Scheduler)
Fresh between sessions too, but it is a new install step on each device, outside Claude.
You asked for no Actions, so freshness has to come from your own machine, and A costs nothing extra.
c2
Which two views?
A
Racetrack + burn-up chart (suggested)
Racetrack shows where work is now; burn-up shows history and the dev/main gap.
B
Hourglass + dependency graph
Hourglass shows the funnel from backlog to shipped; the graph shows which issue blocks which. Needs parent/child links kept clean.
C
Racetrack + milestone timeline
Good if you plan by date; only useful once milestones carry due dates.
The two views answer different questions, and A covers both without extra data.
c3
Where do the views live by default?
A
Local files only (suggested)
Opens from disk in any browser, costs nothing and needs no GitHub setting, but in a cloud session nothing survives the session.
B
Local files plus GitHub Pages from a roadmap-view branch
A shareable web link where hover works. It needs Pages switched on, and I have not verified whether branch-based Pages draws on your Actions allowance.
Both stay available through a setting for each repo; this picks the default for a new repo.
c4
How is the visual-docs page laid out?
A
A new page template for the six sections (suggested)
Reuses make_page.py's colours and pictures but has its own layout. Unlike the current templates, it asks you to approve nothing.
B
Squeeze it into the existing four-part summary page
No new template, but six sections do not fit In short, Changes, Choices and Wrap-up well.
make_page.py's templates are for handover pages that ask for an approval line; an overview asks for none.
c5
Do the roadmap views group by the repo's roadmap milestones?
A
Yes, each view groups dots by the milestones in that repo's docs/2-roadmap/Roadmap.md (suggested)

Keeps the structure each repo's roadmap tier already defines (in this repo, for example, the eight phases decided 2026-11-09). The settings file maps a GitHub milestone or label to each Roadmap.md milestone, and install writes a starter list. A repo with no milestones, or an issue that matches none, is drawn ungrouped, and the view says so in a note.
B
Read #N references under each milestone's Contains list
No mapping to keep, but it only works if the roadmap doc lists issue numbers, which the tier template does not require.
C
Stage only
Simpler, but the views would not show the milestones, and the page would say so.
The roadmap tier is where every house-rules repo defines its milestones, so the views should follow it.
c6
How is the visual-docs page checked for wording?
A
The page check, as for proposals
Hunts for holes, traps and unanswered questions, which suits a design page more than an overview.
B
The editor helper for wording, plus image review of screenshots (suggested)
The editor checks plain English; image review checks how it looks at 375px in light and dark.
C
Style review with the plain-docs rules as the criteria
One review call, but it needs the plain-docs rules written out as criteria text.
An overview is judged on wording and look, not on whether a plan has holes.
c7
When does visual-docs run the review?
A
Once per build, automatically (suggested)

Costs 75 seconds and 50,000 tokens per review (rounded averages of two measured page reviews: 73.8 and 77.2 seconds, 50,353 and 49,615 tokens). A build runs at least two, so 150 seconds and 100,000 tokens at those averages. A page never ships unchecked.
B
Only when you ask: /house-rules:visual-docs review
No cost unless wanted; a page can ship unchecked.
C
Never; rely on visual-loop's own check
Cheapest; skips the page and image reviews entirely.
The page is for people, so a reader's-eye review before it ships is worth the cost.
c8
Where does an issue closed as completed, with no merge naming it, go?
A
Shipped (suggested)
It was finished, so it counts, even if nothing named it in a merge.
B
It leaves the views, like not planned
Keeps Shipped strict to merged work, but hides finished work.
C
It stays in its last stage
Nothing is hidden, but a closed issue sits in Doing or Review for good.
A closed issue should not look unfinished, and the view still shows it as closed.
c9
How are the branch names set?
A
Settings: dev (default dev) and release (default main) (suggested)
One line each in the settings file that install adds. If the dev branch does not exist, the In dev stage is empty and the view says why: no branch named dev was found.
B
Guess the most recently merged-into long-lived branch
No setup, but it can guess wrong when session branches are active.
Repos differ, and this repo has no dev branch, so a guess has nothing reliable to find.
What does visual-docs produce?
A
One page for the whole project (suggested)
A condensed game-design-style overview, as you described.
B
One page per system doc
More detail, but less condensed and more to keep fresh.
Your request was a condensed document, which is one page.

wrapup.summary: A proposal for two new house-rules skills. Visual-docs makes one illustrated overview page from the tier docs. Visual-roadmap is a local script that redraws two roadmap views when issues or merges change, with no GitHub Action of its own and GitHub Pages as an option.
wrapup.changing: Nothing is built. After approval, and once the review command is merged, this adds these things. Two skill folders under claude-house-rules/plugins/house-rules/skills/, where the roadmap one comes with an install command that sets it up in any house-rules repo. One refresh script with its session hook and git hook. In each repo where you run install, a settings file. In this repo, cases in verify.py.
wrapup.blocking: Your approval and ten picks: how fresh the views are, the two views, where views live, how the visual-docs page is checked and when, how the dev branch is found, the docs page scope, the docs page layout, milestone grouping, and where an issue closed without a merge goes.
